title: The body scan
hookLine: moving attention from feet to head, central to Jon Kabat-Zinn's MBSR course (1979), drawn from Buddhist practice

cards: Quick question: how are your feet right now? You probably had to go and check. That's normal.
Most of the day it's easy to live about six inches behind the eyes, with the rest of the body just carrying the head around. It only gets attention when it hurts.
In 1979, in a hospital in Worcester, Massachusetts, a scientist named Jon Kabat-Zinn started a course for patients with chronic pain and illness that doctors had run out of ways to help.
One of the first things he taught them was to lie down and visit their own bodies, one part at a time, starting at the toes.

teach.b: The course was called Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction, MBSR for short, begun at the University of Massachusetts Medical Center. It's eight weeks long, and the body scan sits right at the start.

teach.h: TOES TO THE TOP OF THE HEAD.
teach.b: You lie on your back and move your attention slowly: the toes of the left foot, the sole, the heel, the ankle, up the leg, then the right, the hips, the belly, the back, the hands, the arms, the shoulders, the neck, the face, the top of the head.
At each place you simply notice. Warm, cold, tingling, aching, nothing at all. Nothing at all counts too.
You're not trying to relax, though that often happens.
Kabat-Zinn was open about where he learned this: from Buddhist meditation, which he practiced for years before shaping it for a hospital. The roots go deep.
In the Satipatthana Sutta, the Buddha's great teaching on mindfulness, one exercise is to review this very body from the soles of the feet up, and from the crown of the head down.

The word in Pali is kayagatasati, mindfulness of the body. MBSR set the religious framing aside so anyone could use it, and it's been studied a great deal since, with real but moderate benefits for stress.
You spend all day living in your body.
The scan is a way of showing up there on purpose, and saying, part by part: here I am.

how: In Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction courses, participants practice a guided body scan, usually lying down for about forty-five minutes, moving attention slowly through the body from the feet to the head.

o: mindfulness of the body, part by part
a yoga pose held to stretch the spine
a breathing count used to fall asleep

games.q: what goes with what — tap the pairs.
p: from the soles up, the crown down

s: the goal of the body scan is to relax
the goal is to be there and notice; relaxing often happens, but it isn't the aim.
feeling nothing in a body part counts as noticing
warm, cold, tingling, aching, or nothing at all: all of it counts.
Kabat-Zinn invented the body scan with no outside source
he said openly that he drew it from Buddhist meditation he'd practiced for years.

games.q: you're scanning, and you reach your left knee. it feels like nothing at all. what do you do?
o: keep searching until you feel something.
give up; you're doing it wrong.
games.why: nothing at all counts. you note it and move on. the scan is about showing up, not about finding sensations.

practice: Sitting or lying down, start at your feet and ask what's there, warmth, pressure or nothing, then move up through the legs, the belly rising and falling, the back, the hands, the shoulders, the jaw, the eyes and the top of the head.
Don't fix anything; just visit. At the end, feel the whole body at once, and say inside: here I am.

wordCard.voice: Kayagatasati. The old Pali name for mindfulness of the body, attention moving slowly from the feet to the head, noticing without fixing. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali, kayagatasati: mindfulness (sati) gone to the body (kaya). the old name for attention to the body.

carryVoice: Your line: here I am. Your body is where you live all day. Day one hundred thirty-two, done.

sources.ref: Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction, University of Massachusetts Medical Center (1979)
